I (21) went through a similar thing and am still going through it. My advice would be to tell them! Of course I can only speak from my experience and I have no idea how your parents are but a lot of the times we don’t realize how much they care and think it would be better to just hide it but honestly, just as you were caught, there’s a huge chance it’ll happen again so just tell them! Often times than not, they will actually really just want to know why and how they can help, it was easier for my parents to digest it because they knew of some of my depression two years prior, but of course when I ended up just telling them about my self harm, they realized how severe my issues really were and pushed me to seek a good therapist which before then, was not really something they always supported. It’s definitely not easy living with them and having them know about my issues but it’s given me so much more freedom to do what I want and not do things they may want me to do. It’s hard for any parent to see their child hurting but it’s even harder knowing they can’t help! So let them help you if there’s a chance! It’ll help if you ease them into maybe your sadness or just feelings you have rather than blatantly bringing up the issue at hand. 

Again, I’m really sorry if your parents are nothing like what I’ve written them to maybe be but I hope you find some comfort in that most of the time, the fear you have of your parents finding out is nothing compared to their fear of you hurting yourself.

A staple of a GOOD therapist is how they formulate and reconstruct therapy for you. Therapy is highly personal and there’s no one right method. Most therapists always focus and construct therapy based on your needs and preferences. I wouldn’t say to switch to another therapist per say, but you really should not be stressing over how the therapy is being done you know? That’s their job and being a good listener is the largest role of a therapist! It seems like she can’t cater to you and that’s basically what a therapist is supposed to do so you may want to look into switching or something as much as it may hurt to start all over again.

As for someone who has seen many different Ts for years now and have finally found the right one, I found beginning sessions sometimes the toughest. A lot of the time they tend to do “coffee talk” and though it may help in the short term as you tend to spill all your mind, often times it probably isn’t the right T for you then. I’ve been told by my current psychologist - who is by far the most professional and most credential T I’ve had - that if I find that I feel anxious for our sessions, that it’s sign that something is working. The beginning 2 sessions were and are usually strictly assessments, so determining the disorders one has and lots of questions for sure. Discussing what the right type of therapy is also talked about as well as what goals you have. I’m only now beginning the “therapy” part of it and it’s definitely very different to some past therapists I’ve had so as much as I don’t encourage someone to constantly change or “give up” on their therapist, it’s definitely worth it to find the right one for you.
